historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Fluoride anticaries preparations

starting.description: Long before the Colorado findings, an 1874 preventive proposal drew on a reported animal-enamel observation, and an 1892 address linked fluoride in enamel and diet to a hypothesis about decay. Their connection to the later sodium-fluoride program is unestablished. In the directly documented 20th-century topical lineage, unexpectedly low apparent decay in mottled teeth, fluoride in associated natural waters, and observations in enamel and animals motivated controlled preventive fluoride applications.

inspiration.description: Naturally occurring fluoride in domestic water and observed relationships with caries and enamel, complemented by enamel uptake and animal observations, motivated controlled fluoride exposure in the documented 20th-century lineage. Earlier fluoride-enamel observations and an animal effect were reported alongside separate 19th-century preventive ideas.

steps.description: Before the Colorado work, Erhardt's 1874 preventive recommendation was linked by a later historian to a reported animal-enamel effect, and Crichton-Browne's 1892 address connected enamel fluoride and dietary change to a caries hypothesis. Their continuity to the later topical program is not established.
McKay and Black noted mottling alongside unexpectedly low apparent decay, and the waterborne fluoride explanation was identified later.

Dean compared population exposure and caries, then proposed controlled fluoride use in drinking water; topical researchers later explicitly cited his epidemiology alongside enamel and animal experiments.

Earlier topical work with sodium or potassium fluoride was reported in 1942; Knutson and Armstrong subsequently tested topical sodium fluoride against untreated teeth and a separate untreated group, reporting less new caries after one year.

design.description: Researchers translated observational clues into hypotheses for controlled water exposure and selected and tested a topical sodium-fluoride solution. This was adaptation of fluoride delivery and treatment procedure, not evidence of inventing a new active structure; the authors did not establish an optimum concentration.

circumstances.description: The apparent resistance of mottled teeth was unexpected in the retrospective account; the later controlled-exposure hypotheses and topical trial were deliberate.

limits: The documented observation-led causal chain is strongest for the 20th-century topical sodium-fluoride program; environmental water studies contributed but were not the only observations.

Nineteenth-century fluoride-enamel and preventive proposals predate this chain. Erhardt's reported potassium-fluoride animal finding is not evidence that his proposal caused the later program; the 1892 reprint is selective.

Neither the origin of every oral or topical vehicle nor priority of every fluoride preparation is established; later water fluoridation should not be presented as a prerequisite for the already reported 1942–43 topical studies.
conflicts: A historical review attributes stronger dog enamel to Erhardt's 1874 potassium-fluoride work, but also reports Stubenrauch's 1904 observations of dental and skeletal damage after sodium fluoride. Different conditions are not established and neither original report was read; the claims cannot be directly reconciled here.
gaps: Erhardt's 1874 original article or articles and Stubenrauch's 1904 original were not read; exact methods and continuity to later sodium-fluoride work remain uncertain.
The 1892 Lancet address was read only through a selective 2004 reprint; earlier proposed uses cannot be assigned priority from it.
The 1916 Black–McKay and 1942 Bibby/Cheyne originals and the origins of all later fluoride vehicles were not independently read; accounts are attributed to the sources actually examined.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Lower caries experience in communities with mottled enamel and fluoride-containing water helped motivate fluoride prevention.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: Water chemistry and experimental enamel or animal work also contributed; a population association is not by itself proof of benefit.
